column2: The opening speech addresses Moses; the later house regulations begin a separate address to Moses and Aaron.
The law concerns the day of cleansing and being brought to the priest. The next verse locates their meeting outside camp.
The priest goes outside and observes healing. The ritual procedure follows observed healing rather than claiming the subsequent actions medically cure the lesion.
The priest commands, but plural unnamed people take the birds and materials. Living and clean both qualify the two birds.
The priest commands and they slaughter one bird. Earthenware and living water remain explicit; no water quantity is inserted.
column3: Would fresh or running water better communicate living water here, and what ritual evidence distinguishes them?

column2: The living bird occurs both in the taking list and the dipping clause. That repetition remains rather than being removed as redundant.
Seven sprinklings precede clean status and release of the living bird into the plain. The bird's release location is not generalized away.
Washing, shaving and bathing permit entry into camp, while seven days outside the house remain. House follows the selected Greek, not an imported tent.
The seventh-day shaving names head, beard and eyebrows, then repeats all hair. Garment washing and bodily bathing are distinct.
The Greek names two year-old lambs and one year-old sheep, all unblemished. No explicit female adjective is supplied. Three tenths and one kotyle remain ancient measures.
column3: Should probaton be broader than sheep here, and is the inherited sex-neutral rendering sufficiently precise?

column2: The priest presents the person and the listed items before the Lord at the tent entrance. Both objects are preserved.
One lamb and the oil measure are presented, with separation language. The final neuter object is kept as it rather than resolving its scope silently.
column3: Does the final it collect both gifts or focus on one offering?

column2: Slaughter is plural; the location is holy. The Greek compares the sin offering with the guilt offering in that order and assigns it to the priest.
Blood goes on the right ear and right hand/foot extremities. Broad extremity terminology is consistent with the earlier consecration passage.
Oil is poured onto the priest's left hand. The repeated priest designation does not by itself establish a second officiant.
The right finger takes oil from the left hand for seven sprinklings. Right and left are not interchangeable details.
Oil is placed at the three right-side sites, on the place of the guilt-offering blood. The place phrase is explicit.
Remaining oil goes on the cleansed person's head; priestly atonement follows. The two actions remain distinct.
The Greek describes cleansing from his sin here and explicitly names the priest as slaughterer afterward. Neither detail is harmonized away.
Whole offering and sacrifice are offered on the altar before the Lord; atonement and cleansing conclude the sequence.
Poverty and insufficient means allow one lamb, one tenth of flour and one oil measure. Reduced flour quantity is retained.
Two turtledoves or two young pigeons depend on available means. Their sin-offering and whole-offering roles remain separate.
The eighth day and tent entrance apply to presenting the reduced gifts for cleansing. Before the Lord remains explicit.
The lamb and oil are placed as a presentation. Epithema differs from the separation noun earlier; the inherited distinction is provisional.
The singular slaughter contrasts with the plural in verse 13. Blood goes to the same three right-side sites.
Oil is again poured onto the priest's left hand; the repeated ritual detail is retained in the reduced-offering procedure.
Seven sprinklings use the right finger and oil in the left hand. No abbreviated cross-reference replaces the full instruction.
Oil is put at the ear, hand and foot sites where blood was placed. The repeated possessives remain understandable without expanding their antecedents.
Remaining oil is placed on the head, followed by atonement. The one performing the placement is implicit before the priest is named.
The source says one of the birds here, followed by one and one in verse 31. The awkward coordination is retained without changing the number.
column3: How should the two-verse construction express preparation of both birds while respecting mian here?

column2: One bird is for sin and one for the whole offering, with the sacrifice accompanying. Priest and cleansed person remain distinct.
The summary includes the lesion-bearing person and the person lacking means for cleansing. The conjunction is retained rather than rewritten as an exclusive class.
The new speech explicitly addresses both Moses and Aaron, beginning the house procedure.
The Lord gives the land and puts the lesion in houses. Divine agency in both clauses remains explicit.
The owner reports something like a lesion, preserving uncertainty before priestly examination. He does not pronounce the house unclean himself.
Emptying precedes inspection to prevent contents becoming unclean. The sequence and purpose remain, without treating emptying as a structural repair.
Greenish or reddish hollows appear lower than the wall surface. The colours are alternatives and the depth comparison remains.
The priest leaves for the door and isolates the house seven days. The house, rather than its owner, is the object.
The selected Greek expressly says the lesion has not spread. This surprising negative is retained before the removal order, not silently corrected.
column3: Apparatus review is needed for the negative; no variant is substituted in this draft.

column2: Unnamed plural workers remove affected stones at the priest's command and discard them outside the city in an unclean place.
Interior scraping all around is followed by removal of dust outside the city. The disposal location remains repeated.
Replacement stones are described as scraped; other earth is used for replastering. The source adjective is not omitted.
Again is warranted by palin; recurrence follows removal, scraping and plastering. All three completed stages remain.
The priest examines recurrence and spreading, and persistent leprosy renders the house unclean. No modern mould species is specified.
Demolition and removal include timbers, stones and all dust. The repeated outside-city unclean location remains.
Entering during isolation entails uncleanness until evening. The duration differs from the house's seven-day isolation.
Both sleeping and eating require garment washing and uncleanness until evening in this Greek text. The repeated duration is retained.
The emphatic no-spreading expression supports not spread at all. After plastering, healing grounds the priest's clean declaration.
Two living clean birds and the same three materials are taken to purify the house. Both bird qualifications are explicit.
One bird is slaughtered into earthenware over living water. The singular agent is not changed to the earlier plural workers.
The dipping object is singular it after the list, while sprinkling uses plural them. The inherited number shift is preserved pending syntactic review.
column3: Does singular auto refer specifically to the bird or to the combined implement?

column2: All six means of purification are listed, including both blood and water and the living bird. None is reduced to an implied instrument.
The bird is released outside the city into the plain. Atonement concerns the house, which becomes clean.
The closing law includes every lesion and broken patch. The inherited thrausma label remains provisional as in chapter 13.
Garments and houses both fall within the broad ancient lepra category. This is not a modern medical classification.
Scar, mark and shining spot remain three descriptions rather than a single generalized blemish.
Explanation concerns the day of uncleanness and the day of cleansing. The final law formula closes the whole section.
The Lord addresses Moses and Aaron together; the next command is grammatically singular despite this joint introduction.
Any man represents the distributive repeated noun. The bodily flow itself is called unclean; no modern diagnosis is inserted.
Seed, flow and the stopped-up condition follow the selected Greek's difficult repeated syntax. The repetition is not replaced with a simpler foreign base.
column3: Confirm sunesteken and the causal/relative construction: stopped up, congealed or another contextual sense?

column2: The Greek identifies a seminal-discharge sufferer; both bed and seating article become unclean. The term is not treated as a modern disease name.
Touching the bed requires garment washing, bathing and waiting until evening. All three prescriptions remain.
Sitting on the affected article receives the same three prescriptions. Its prior use by the sufferer is explicit.
Direct skin contact has its own rule. Skin is retained rather than an unspecified personal proximity.
The clean person spat upon washes and bathes. That person clarifies the change of subject without assigning those actions to the sufferer.
The Greek explicitly names a donkey saddle and until evening. The animal and duration are not omitted.
Touching and carrying differ: carrying requires washing and bathing as well as the time limit. Both rules remain.
Unwashed hands belong to the sufferer who touches another person. The touched person receives the washing and bathing requirement.
Earthenware is broken; wood is washed and becomes clean. The concluding clean declaration is explicit in this source.
After cessation/cleansing of the flow, seven days precede washing and bathing. The Greek here says water without an added living adjective.
The eighth-day pair of birds is given to the priest at the tent doors. Doors is plural in the selected text.
One bird is for sin and one for the whole offering; atonement is connected with the flow. The force of apo remains a translation question.
column3: Does from his flow better represent the relation than inherited for his flow?

column2: An emission of semen requires washing the entire body and remaining unclean until evening. Entire is explicitly supported.
Both garment and skin material bearing semen are washed. Skin denotes an article here in context, not a second command to bathe the man.
The sexual act involving emission requires both people to bathe. The plural verbs prevent assigning the prescription only to the woman.
The woman's seven-day condition differs from the until-evening condition of a person touching her. The two durations remain distinct.
Both lying and sitting surfaces become unclean during the discharge. No bodily washing command is imported into this verse.
Touching the bed requires washing garments, bathing the body and waiting until evening. The bodily object is explicit.
Touching a seating article has a parallel prescription. The repeated washing requirements are retained in full.
The Greek locates the woman on bed or article while someone touches her. The feminine pronoun is not replaced by contact with the objects alone.
Intercourse with transmission of her uncleanness yields seven days, and his bed becomes unclean. The longer duration is preserved.
Prolonged bleeding outside the usual time or afterward receives the same unclean status. The two time conditions remain distinguishable.
Beds and seating articles during the prolonged flow are treated like those during the menstrual period. The full comparison remains.
The Greek object is her, not them. Direct contact leads to washing, bathing and uncleanness until evening.
A first cleansing from the flow is followed by counting seven days and subsequent cleansing. The apparent repetition marks stages rather than an editorial duplicate.
On the eighth day the woman brings two birds to the priest at the tent entrance. The action remains hers.
The priest prepares separate sin and whole offerings and makes atonement concerning the unclean flow. The apo relation parallels verse 15 and remains open.
Make wary reflects the eulabes expression; death is linked to defiling the divine tent among them. The plural addressees return here.
The summary distinguishes the ongoing discharge category from an emission of semen. Neither is collapsed into a named modern disease.
The summary includes menstrual bleeding, discharge in male or female, and intercourse with a woman in separation. Seminal discharge is lexically awkward with the expanded female scope.
column3: Should gonorrues here receive the broader discharging person while earlier male contexts retain their specificity?
